title: Bones of the upper limb (anterior)
attribution: 3D anatomy from Z-Anatomy, built on BodyParts3D (CC BY-SA). Rendered in Blender; surface detail added with an image model.

rows: S-shaped bone that lies horizontally at the root of the neck and connects the upper limb to the trunk.
Manubrium of the sternum at its medial end and the acromion of the scapula at its lateral end.
The medial two-thirds are convex forward and the lateral third is flattened. Conoid tubercle and trapezoid line for the coracoclavicular ligament.
hy: The most often fractured bone, usually in its middle third. Its weakest point is where the middle and lateral thirds meet. Sternocleidomastoid pulls the medial piece up and the weight of the arm drags the lateral piece down.

rows: Flat triangular bone on the back of the chest wall, over ribs 2 to 7.
Head of the humerus at the glenoid cavity and the clavicle at the acromion.
Spine, acromion, coracoid process, glenoid cavity, suprascapular notch, and the supraspinous, infraspinous and subscapular fossae.
hy: When serratus anterior is paralyzed by injury to the long thoracic nerve, the medial border of the scapula lifts off the chest wall (winged scapula).

rows: Glenoid cavity of the scapula above; the radius and the ulna at the elbow.
Head, anatomical and surgical necks, greater and lesser tubercles, deltoid tuberosity, radial groove, capitulum, trochlea, medial and lateral epicondyles.
hy: Three nerves lie against the bone and are injured by fractures at those sites: the axillary nerve at the surgical neck, the radial nerve in the radial groove at midshaft, and the ulnar nerve behind the medial epicondyle.
A supracondylar fracture, common in children, threatens the brachial artery and the median nerve.

rows: Lateral bone of the forearm, on the side of the thumb.
Capitulum of the humerus, the ulna at its upper and lower ends, and the scaphoid and lunate at the wrist.
Head, neck, radial tuberosity, dorsal tubercle, styloid process.
hy: A fall on the outstretched hand breaks its distal end, with the broken piece displaced toward the back of the wrist (Colles fracture).
In a young child a sudden pull on the arm can slip the head of the radius out of the annular ligament (nursemaid's elbow).

rows: Medial bone of the forearm, on the side of the little finger.
Trochlea of the humerus, and the radius at its upper and lower ends. An articular disc separates it from the carpal bones.
Olecranon, coronoid process, trochlear notch, radial notch, head (at its lower end), styloid process.
The eight bones of the wrist, in two rows of four.
Proximal row from lateral to medial: scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform. Distal row from lateral to medial: trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate.
hy: A common mnemonic, proximal row from lateral to medial and then distal row from medial to lateral: So Long To Pinky, Here Comes The Thumb.

The scaphoid is the carpal bone most often fractured, in a fall on the outstretched hand, with tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox. Its proximal piece may lose its blood supply and die (avascular necrosis).

rows: The five bones of the palm, between the carpal bones and the fingers, numbered 1 to 5 from the thumb.
Each has a base, a shaft and a head. The heads form the knuckles.
hy: A punch with a closed fist typically breaks the neck of the fifth metacarpal (boxer's fracture).

rows: The bones of the thumb and fingers.
Fourteen in all. The thumb has two, a proximal and a distal phalanx. Each finger has three: proximal, middle and distal.
